newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindu party suffers setback in state polls.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindu party suffers setback in state polls.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition got a boost on Thursday when the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party failed to win an outright majority in India's most populous state, Uttar Pradesh.

"The significant aspect of the elections is that people have set their face against the BJP, which wanted to divide the people on religious and other sectarian issues," Gowda told the United News of India agency.

With results declared in 392 of 425 races in the state assembly, the right-wing BJP was leading in a triangular race with 163 seats but falling short of an absolute majority. In the last state election in 1993, the BJP won 176 seats.
"We accept the defeat," BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee told reporters in the state capital Lucknow.

The partial returns showed Deve Gowda's United Front coalition had won 118 races, while an alliance between the Congress party and its low-cast partner, the Hindu Bahujan Samaj Party or BSP, had taken 99.
Other parties had clinched 12 seats.
"We have done well to keep BJP away from power," said Ram Saran Das, state chief of the Samajwadi Party, a coalition partner in Gowda's ruling United Front.
The BJP, which built its national foundations on a Hindu revivalist agenda in Uttar Pradesh in the late 1980s, had hoped to win control of India's biggest electoral prize.
Instead, the United Front and the Congress-BSP alliance were already jockeying to rule the sprawling state with 140 million people.
"We have fallen far below our expections," BJP state chief Kalraj Misra said.
The polls had signficance for Deve Gowda's stability in New Delhi because his centre-left coalition there depends on the Congress to survive against a BJP challenge in parliament.
Congress has insisted that the United Front back its candidate for chief minister in Uttar Pradesh, BSP leader Mayawati.
"We are committed to Mayawati," state Congress president Jitendra Prasada.
But the United Front's main component in Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party, wants its leader and Deve Gowda's defence minister, Mulayam Singh Yadav, to lead the state.

The tensions in Uttar Pradesh have spilled over to New Delhi, where the Congress party's new chief Sitaram Kesri recently threatened to withdraw support for Deve Gowda unless his coalition backed the Congress-BSP alliance in the state.
"There is no reason why they (United Front) shouldn't support Mayawati if they're truly anti-communal," State Congress leader Prasada said.
The BJP's rivals call the Hindu nationalist party "communal" because they claim it alienates minority Moslems.

The BJP appeared to be manoeuvring to try to draw Congress away from the United Front. "We know we are far short of a majority and therefore we have to look for other options," BJP leader Pramod Mahajan said.
"Let a government be formed with our support. Our doors are open."
Congress, however, rejected the possibility of allying itself with the BJP. "We will have no direct or indirect truck with the BJP," Prasada said.
